prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators

statement.case_for: B050 has the broadest support across the table, with six members ranking it and three placing it in their top three. It is a clean sequence of theory and experiment. Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal in 2005, and Molenkamp's group observed edge-channel transport in HgTe quantum wells in 2007. Two decades on, the result has been confirmed independently by transport, ARPES and first-principles band-structure work, and the concept now organises a large part of materials physics. That is the kind of verified, reproducible discovery I weigh most, and it is a new state of electronic matter that nature made available only once theory told us where to look. The recognition is overdue rather than premature.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely awkward. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal pointed to HgTe, and Molenkamp's experiment tested that proposal. The three-dimensional topological insulators (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hasan and Cava) are also only partly covered by these names. The 2016 prize for topological phases may make some colleagues see this as a second helping of the same theme. Practical applications, such as dissipationless edge transport, have not materialised, so the case rests on conceptual and scientific impact. That is acceptable for the prize, but it would be weaker if the committee demands an applied payoff.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B050 fourth and sees no doubt about maturity. She worries that the missing theorists around the HgTe proposal make the fair configuration awkward, and she suggests the committee consider splitting the 2D and 3D steps.
responses.response: I share the concern about Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and I do not think it can be dismissed. But I would answer it differently. The Kane-Mele paper preceded the HgTe proposal and supplied the invariant and the model, and BHZ built on that framework to identify the material. Molenkamp's experiment is the decisive test, so the prize citation can honestly reflect that chain. Splitting 2D and 3D would stretch one prize into two topics. I would keep the citation narrow on the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, and accept that the 3D discoverers fall outside a three-person limit.

responses.point: Kroll puts optical lattice clocks first because they are the clearest new measurement capability, with the Katori-Ye pair compact and defensible and the field mature.
responses.response: I agree the clock case is strong on reproducibility, since many national laboratories agree at the 1e-18 level, and that is a point in its favour that I take seriously. Where I differ is on the novelty of the discovery. The prize has already gone to frequency combs in 2005 and ion clocks in 2012, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. For me this is a good second choice, but it carries more of an incremental-precision flavour than a new state of matter. I would not object if the committee preferred it, and I do not regard the gap between the two as large.

responses.point: Lindroth places B050 sixth. She regards it as a genuinely new state of matter with a good theory-experiment match, but she points to the missing BHZ names and to overlap with the 2016 prize.
responses.response: The 2016 overlap needs a direct answer. That prize honoured topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall effect, and the Haldane and Kosterlitz-Thouless ideas it recognised. Z2 time-reversal-invariant topology, protected by spin-orbit coupling without a magnetic field, is physically distinct, and it is the version that led to materials work. I would ask her whether the missing BHZ credit is serious enough to push B050 below the clocks for her, because I think that is where our difference lies, rather than on the science.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B050 seventh, and says he defers to the condensed-matter colleagues. He notes that dissipationless transport has been limited in practice and that the 3D contributors are missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I take the deference as a fair request for the condensed-matter members to carry the argument, so I should be explicit. On limited applications, I agree the practical hopes have been disappointing, but quantised edge transport and ARPES-resolved surface states are robust, reproducible observations, and a prize for a discovery does not depend on a device. I accept that 3D topological insulators are a separate step, and the committee may need an expert report on how the credit should be drawn. I would ask him for a view on B038, since he knows that field far better than I do, and I do not want my lean to hide a recusal issue there.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B009 first and B050 second, praising the sharp prediction tested by a decisive HgTe experiment. He flags the BHZ proposal as an unresolved fairness issue.
responses.response: We agree on the science and on the main difficulty. The one thing I would add to his reading is that confirmation is not limited to a single experiment, because the HgTe result has since been supplemented by 3D materials and spectroscopy. I read the IceCube discovery as important but outside my own expertise, and I defer to him and Pearce on its maturity. My main reservation is whether one laureate for a collaboration-scale detector is workable, which Pearce raised himself. If the committee cannot settle that, I would not want to see B050 lose out because of a standoff.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a three-person credit that leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and whether an outside expert report would change the allocation.
Whether the 3D topological insulator work should be named in the citation or left outside it.
How much the 2016 topological-phase prize weighs against a second topological prize within a decade.
Relative merit of B050 against B051 and B027, where I rely on AMO and precision-measurement colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B050, B051 or B002. I have no recorded connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. My theory-based work on electronic structure is close in field to B050 and B002, but that is not a personal or institutional connection.
